facts.text: Le nozze di Figaro premiered at the Burgtheater in Vienna on 1 May 1786.
facts.evidence: It premiered at the Burgtheater in Vienna on 1 May 1786.

facts.text: Beaumarchais’s play was at first banned in Vienna for its frank treatment of class conflict; Da Ponte won the emperor’s approval for an opera version.
evidence: with its frank treatment of class conflict, was at first banned in Vienna
Lorenzo Da Ponte managed to get official approval from the emperor for an operatic version

facts.text: It was Mozart who picked Beaumarchais’s play. Da Ponte turned it into a libretto in six weeks, removing all of the political references.
facts.evidence: It was Mozart who originally selected Beaumarchais's play and brought it to Da Ponte, who turned it into a libretto in six weeks, rewriting it in poetic Italian and removing all of the original's political references

facts.sceneMatch: Aprite un po|Tutto è disposto|Tutto e disposto
facts.text: Da Ponte swapped Figaro’s angry speech against inherited nobility for an equally angry aria against unfaithful wives.
facts.evidence: Da Ponte replaced Figaro's climactic speech against inherited nobility with an equally angry aria against unfaithful wives

facts.text: Mozart uses two horns playing together here to represent cuckoldry. Verdi later borrowed the same trick in Falstaff.
evidence: Mozart uses the sound of two horns playing together to represent cuckoldry in the act 4 aria "Aprite un po' quegli occhi"
Verdi later used the same device in Ford's aria in Falstaff.

facts.text: The first-night audience demanded encores of five numbers; on 8 May, seven.
facts.evidence: The applause of the audience on the first night resulted in five numbers being encored, seven on 8 May.

facts.text: Worried about the running time, Emperor Joseph II ordered posters announcing that no piece for more than a single voice was to be repeated.
evidence: Emperor Joseph, in charge of the Burgtheater, was concerned by the length of the performance
no piece for more than a single voice is to be repeated

facts.text: A 1786 Vienna review: Mozart’s music was admired by connoisseurs, but “obstreperous louts in the uppermost storey” tried to drown out the singers.
evidence: Mozart's music was generally admired by connoisseurs already at the first performance
obstreperous louts in the uppermost storey exerted their hired lungs with all their might to deafen singers and audience alike

facts.text: In Prague the opera caused a sensation; a local paper wrote that “no piece … has ever caused such a sensation.” That success led to the commission of Don Giovanni.
evidence: no piece (for everyone here asserts) has ever caused such a sensation
The success of the Prague production led to the commissioning of the next Mozart/Da Ponte opera, Don Giovanni

facts.text: The Act II finale runs about 20 minutes, one of the longest uninterrupted pieces of music Mozart ever wrote.
facts.evidence: The finale of act 2, lasting 20 minutes, is one of the longest uninterrupted pieces of music Mozart ever wrote.

facts.text: Brahms: “In my opinion, each number in Figaro is a miracle … nothing like it was ever done again, not even by Beethoven.”
evidence: In my opinion, each number in Figaro is a miracle
nothing like it was ever done again, not even by Beethoven

facts.text: Mozart liked this tune enough to quote “Non più andrai” in the second act of Don Giovanni.
facts.evidence: Mozart also quotes Figaro's aria "Non più andrai" in the second act of his opera Don Giovanni.

facts.text: “Porgi, amor” reuses the motif that opens Mozart’s early bassoon concerto.
facts.evidence: Mozart also reused the motif that begins his early bassoon concerto in another aria sung by the countess, "Porgi, amor".

facts.sceneMatch: Cosa sento|Così fan tutte|Cosi fan tutte
facts.text: Basilio’s phrase “Così fan tutte le belle” in this trio later turned up in the overture to Mozart’s Così fan tutte.
facts.evidence: A musical phrase from the act 1 trio of The Marriage of Figaro (where Basilio sings Così fan tutte le belle) was later reused by Mozart in the overture to his opera Così fan tutte.

facts.text: Beethoven wrote a set of variations for violin and piano on Figaro’s “Se vuol ballare”.
facts.evidence: Beethoven wrote Variations on 'Se vuol ballare', WoO 40, for violin and piano on Figaro's cavatina.

facts.text: For a 1789 revival Mozart wrote two replacement arias for Susanna. The Met used them in 1998, with Cecilia Bartoli as Susanna.
evidence: Mozart wrote two replacement arias for Susanna when the role was taken over by Adriana Ferrarese in the 1789 revival
A notable exception was a series of performances at the Metropolitan Opera in 1998 with Cecilia Bartoli as Susanna.
